title: *Visual mode* as a learning tool
subtitle: Use {key:v} to see motions, select familiar ranges, and build confidence.
summary: {key:v} enters character-wise *visual mode.* Motions extend a visible selection, making this a useful bridge from other editors and a way to learn what motions do.

blocks.text: Most editors teach you to select text first and choose an action second. Vim supports that familiar order. Press {key:v} in *normal mode* to enter character-wise *visual mode.* Move the cursor, and the text between your starting point and the cursor is highlighted. Press {key:d} to delete the selection, {key:y} to yank it, or {key:c} to replace it.

blocks.label: Select with a word motion, then delete

blocks.text: Press {key:Esc} to cancel the selection and return to *normal mode.* Pressing {key:v} again also leaves character-wise *visual mode.*

*Visual mode* is a useful laboratory for motions. Start a selection with {key:v}, try a motion, and watch where the cursor lands. {key:w} moves toward the next word, {key:e} moves to a word ending, {key:$} reaches the end of the line, and {key:G} reaches the end of the file. The highlight makes the direction and scale of each motion visible. Press {key:Esc}, return to the starting point, and try another.

blocks.text: The highlight shows where a motion travels, but it is not always a byte-for-byte preview of an operator followed by that motion. Motions can be inclusive, exclusive, or linewise, and operators honor those shapes. [Motion Classification](#appendix.motion-classification) explains the edge cases.

Selection-first editing is useful, especially while learning, but it is not usually the shortest Vim path. Vim's native grammar puts the operator first and the motion second. Instead of selecting a word and then deleting it, press {key:d}{key:w}. Instead of selecting the word under the cursor and then copying it, press {key:y}{key:i}{key:w}. Instead of selecting to the end of the line and then replacing it, press {key:c}{key:$}.

Nothing flashes on the screen before those commands act. You learn to trust the motion. The operator and motion resolve the range together, without creating a visible selection first. This is faster, composes with counts, and records one clean action for the dot command.

Use *visual mode* when you need reassurance, when the range is irregular, or when seeing the selection helps you decide. As a motion becomes familiar, remove the preview. Trust the motion by itself, then replace select-then-act with an operator followed directly by that motion.
